theory.title: VLANs: The Logical Divide
theory.recap: You've routed across IP subnets and passed through firewalls. Now you meet a different boundary - VLANs. A switched network keeps segments apart even when they share hardware, and the only way across is a Layer-3 device that still uses the same routing-table rules you've been reading since Level 1.
theory.plainObjective: Find the Layer-3 switch and use its routing table to bridge VLAN 10 and VLAN 20. Longest-prefix match still decides.
theory.summary: Every corporate network, university, and data centre uses VLANs to isolate traffic. The pattern you just followed - blocked direct path, route via L3 device - happens millions of times a day.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Switches don't route
bodyParagraphs.text: A standard Layer-2 switch forwards frames using MAC addresses within the same network segment. It has no concept of subnets or IP routing. Connect a device to VLAN 10 and a device to VLAN 20 on the same physical switch and they will not talk - the switch keeps them separate by design.

bodyParagraphs.heading: What is a VLAN?
bodyParagraphs.text: VLAN (Virtual LAN) is a way to logically partition a network. Ports on a switch are assigned to a VLAN number. Traffic from VLAN 10 stays in VLAN 10. Even if all devices share the same physical hardware, VLANs create isolated broadcast domains - as if they were on completely different physical switches.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Why segment?
bodyParagraphs.text: Organisations put different kinds of devices on different VLANs: IoT devices on VLAN 10, servers on VLAN 20, guest Wi-Fi on VLAN 30. If a device on the IoT VLAN is compromised, it cannot reach the server VLAN directly. Segmentation turns a flat network into a series of contained zones. Isolation is security.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Inter-VLAN routing
bodyParagraphs.text: To move traffic between VLANs you need a Layer-3 device with an interface in each VLAN. Its routing table follows the exact same rules you've been using: match the destination prefix, longest one wins. The L3 switch here has three overlapping routes - the new wrinkle is that it bridges VLANs, but the decision rule is unchanged.

theory.mission: You're 10.10.0.5 on VLAN 10. The destination 10.20.0.10 is on VLAN 20. Direct crossing is blocked - find the L3 switch and let its routing table pick the most specific route to VLAN 20.

termIntroductions.headline: VLAN
termIntroductions.body: You are on VLAN 10 - a logical network segment. VLANs partition a physical network so traffic from one segment cannot reach another directly. Your destination is on VLAN 20. A standard switch will not forward your packet across the boundary.

termIntroductions.headline: VLAN Isolation
termIntroductions.body: Traffic cannot cross this boundary without being routed. There is no port rule here - the switch simply has no path between VLAN 10 and VLAN 20. You need a Layer-3 device to cross between segments.

termIntroductions.headline: Inter-VLAN Routing
termIntroductions.body: A Layer-3 switch has one logical interface in each VLAN. It routes packets between them using its routing table - just like a router. Three overlapping prefixes - one is a /24 covering your destination, one is a /8 covering the whole campus, one is your home VLAN. Longest prefix wins.
